summary: This informational document defines Opportunistic Security: protocols use encryption even when authentication is not available, and use authentication when possible. The goal is to remove barriers to widespread encryption, giving some protection most of the time instead of none.

plainLanguage.summary: Locking your door is better than leaving it open, even if you cannot check who knocks. Opportunistic security says to scramble messages whenever you can, and check identities when you can too.

questions: why not require authentication for encryption
subtitle: Encrypt whenever both sides can, authenticate whenever possible, and stop treating cleartext as the only alternative to perfect.

tldr.problem: Security protocols that insist on full authenticated encryption often fail or get switched off, so most Internet traffic ends up in cleartext.
tldr.mechanism: Opportunistic Security takes cleartext as the baseline and negotiates encryption and then authentication with each peer when available, never overriding an explicit security policy.
tldr.outcome: Passive monitoring becomes harder and more selective, while communication keeps working with peers that support less.

facts.label: Possible outcomes
facts.value: 3 (authenticated and encrypted, unauthenticated but encrypted, cleartext)

today: RFC 7435 is an Informational document published in December 2014, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes a design approach rather than a protocol.

sections.title: The All-or-Nothing Problem
sections.content:
Internet security protocols have historically offered comprehensive protection against both passive and active attacks. With each peer the result is either full protection or a hard failure to communicate. Operators therefore often disable the protection when users have trouble connecting, and everything degrades to cleartext.

Protection against active attacks needs authentication, and the RFC argues nothing scales to authenticate every possible peer. The Web PKI has many Certification Authorities that not everyone trusts, and expired certificates and constant warnings teach users to ignore them. Trust on first use (TOFU) does not protect the first contact. DANE needs DNSSEC, which at the time of writing was not widely enough deployed.

The result is that most traffic is cleartext, which makes pervasive monitoring cheap. The RFC concludes that authentication needs to be optional if encryption is to be used more broadly.
sections.plainLanguage: If the only choices are a perfect lock or no lock, many people give up and use nothing. Letting people use a good-enough lock means far more doors get locked.

sections.title: A New Perspective and Key Terms
sections.content:
Opportunistic Security (OS) is defined as using cleartext as the baseline communication security policy, with encryption and authentication negotiated and applied when available. An OS protocol is not falling back from comprehensive protection; it aims for the maximum protection that is available. A session can end up authenticated and encrypted, unauthenticated but encrypted, or cleartext.

The RFC defines the terms it relies on. Authenticated, encrypted communication means at least the client authenticates the server's identity. Unauthenticated, encrypted communication does not authenticate the peers, so MiTM attacks remain possible. Trust on First Use (TOFU) accepts and stores a key without authenticating it, as the SSH protocol does in its commonly deployed form. Encryption mitigates passive monitoring, and authentication mitigates active MiTM attacks.

When only partial protection is negotiated, OS says there is no need to prompt the user with "your security may be degraded" dialogs.
sections.plainLanguage: The starting point is saying nothing secret, and every extra step up (scrambling, then checking who you are talking to) is a bonus rather than a downgrade.

sections.title: The Design Principles
sections.content:
OS promotes four principles:

  • Coexist with explicit policy. Explicit security policies preempt OS, and many applications and types of data are too sensitive to use it.
  • Prioritize communication. OS must not impede communication and must be deployable incrementally, peer by peer.
  • Maximize security peer by peer. Use encryption when mutually supported, authenticate when an authenticated out-of-band channel supplies the keys, and use perfect forward secrecy (PFS) wherever possible.
  • No misrepresentation of security. Unauthenticated, encrypted communication must not be presented to users or logs as equivalent to authenticated, encrypted communication.

A peer's capabilities can be found out of band (DANE records, or keys cached through TOFU) or in band by negotiation. If authentication is "expected" by a downgrade-resistant method (validated DANE records, existing TOFU information, or manual configuration), the protocol should produce authenticated, encrypted communication. Otherwise default authentication checks must be disabled or set to soft-fail. A protocol may use more liberal cryptographic settings for unauthenticated sessions and stricter ones for authenticated sessions. It may hard-fail if an advertised capability does not work, so advertised capabilities need to match what is deployed.
sections.plainLanguage: Use the best lock the other side has, never be sneaky about how strong it is, and never stop an important rule from winning over this relaxed approach.

sections.title: Example: Opportunistic TLS in SMTP
sections.content:
Most mail transfer agents support the STARTTLS extension (RFC 3207). An SMTP client sends cleartext unless the server announces STARTTLS support, and because the initial negotiation is not protected, the announcement can be stripped by a MiTM downgrade attack. The RFC treats that as a reasonable trade-off, since STARTTLS only protects against passive attacks. It cites reports from large providers that the majority of SMTP email is now encrypted.

Some behaviors are NOT consistent with OS principles: clients that abandon the TLS handshake as soon as the server fails authentication and go to cleartext, or that accept unverified self-signed certificates but not expired ones and then fall back to cleartext. Both needlessly use cleartext when encryption is possible. The RFC points to "Opportunistic DANE TLS", where authenticated, encrypted communication is enforced for peers with appropriate DANE records and plain Opportunistic TLS is used for the rest.
sections.plainLanguage: Email servers already do this: they scramble mail when both ends can, and send it plainly otherwise. The mistake is giving up on scrambling just because the other side's ID card looks odd.

sections.title: Operational and Security Considerations
sections.content:
OS designs should minimize the chance that negotiated security fails. Fallback to cleartext should be enabled only in response to significant operational obstacles, because failure to encrypt is often an interoperability problem rather than an attack. If problems are frequent, administrators may simply disable OS.

The RFC argues that OS does not reduce the security anyone gets: it uses the best services available and explicit policy takes precedence. Large-scale passive monitors can no longer just collect everything, and active attacks on everyone all the time are much more likely to be noticed. Some protocols that could support OS may face low-cost downgrade attacks from attackers on the path, but pervasive use of those attacks is often detectable. Techniques for detecting active attacks without authentication are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: If a few messages go out unlocked when a lock jams, that is better than people turning off locks altogether. Also, snoops now have to pick targets instead of copying everything.

viz.caption: THE THREE POSSIBLE OUTCOMES OF OPPORTUNISTIC SECURITY

items.title: Authenticated and encrypted
items.text: Protects against passive and active attacks.

items.title: Unauthenticated but encrypted
items.text: Protects against passive monitoring; MiTM attacks stay possible.

items.title: Cleartext
items.text: The baseline, used when a peer supports nothing more.
